title: Tetris's Soviet origin
hook: The world's best-known puzzle game was written at a Soviet research institute.
peek: Tetris was created in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov, a researcher at a Soviet computing centre in Moscow. It spread on copied floppy disks, sparked a tangled fight over the rights, and earned its inventor nothing for years.
lede: In 1984 Alexey Pajitnov was working at the Dorodnitsyn Computing Centre of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow, testing a computer called the Electronika 60. In his spare time he wrote a puzzle game where falling shapes fill rows that then vanish. The machine had no graphics, so the first pieces were drawn with brackets and other text characters.

bullets.text: Pajitnov was inspired by pentomino puzzles, made from shapes of five squares. He used four-square pieces instead, which gave seven shapes that were simpler to rotate on screen.
The name joins tetra, Greek for four, with tennis, Pajitnov's favourite sport.

Copies travelled across the Soviet Union and then to the West. Because software belonged to the state, rights had to be negotiated through a state agency, and several companies ended up believing they owned the same game.
Henk Rogers, a Dutch-born game designer, secured handheld rights for Nintendo. Tetris came packaged with the Game Boy in North America in 1989, with a Russian folk tune, Korobeiniki, as its music.
For years Pajitnov earned nothing from his game. That changed in 1996, when he and Rogers set up The Tetris Company and he began receiving royalties.
